hook: The philosopher who wrote "Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains".

pages.x: Rousseau was born in Geneva in 1712; his mother died days later. At 15, coming back from a walk to find the city gates shut for the night, he ran away rather than face his master's punishment.
He drifted through Savoy, Italy and France as a servant, music teacher and secretary, sheltered for years by a kind patroness. He invented a new way of writing music and moved to Paris in 1742.

In 1749, walking to visit a friend in prison, he read about an essay contest: had the arts and sciences made people better? In a flash he saw that people are good by nature and society corrupts them. He sat under a tree and wept. His essay won the prize and made him famous.

In 1762 he wrote The Social Contract, which begins: "Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains." Laws, he argued, should express the will of the whole people. Its ideas inspired the French Revolution.
In Emile, the same year, he said children should learn from nature and experience, not by rote and beatings. It changed ideas about childhood. Both books were burned, and he had to flee.
The man who wrote about raising children left all five of his own, with his partner Thérèse, at a home for foundlings, where most children died. His enemies made sure everyone knew.

In his last years he grew suspicious of everyone and wrote his Confessions, a frank story of his life. He died in 1778. Sixteen years later the revolutionaries moved his body to the Panthéon in Paris.
Rousseau's ideas on freedom, equality and the will of the people inspired the French Revolution and modern democracy, and his love of nature and feeling helped start the Romantic movement.
pts: Changed ideas about childhood and education
